newsitem.title: USA: Americans upbeat on stocks as long-haul investment.
newsitem.headline: Americans upbeat on stocks as long-haul investment.

text.p: American investors are more cautious than euphoric about stocks despite the long-running bull market but most say they would not bail out in case of a sharp downturn, a survey said Friday.

The survey, conducted for the Nasdaq stock market by Peter D. Hart Research Associates, showed that 63 percent of investors expected stock prices to rise over the next 12 months, with 58 percent anticipating a moderate increase and 20 percent a strong increase.
The new findings revealed that stock ownership has grown dramatically and that stocks have attracted a diverse lot of investors.

Some 43 percent of Americans said they own stock in mutual funds or in individual companies other than the ones they work for, or both. That's roughly double the 21 percent of the population that owned stock in 1990.

A majority of investors are younger than 50 -- the Baby Boomers, their younger brothers and sisters and their children; half lack a college degree, 47 percent are women and two-thirds call themselves non-professionals. Nearly two in five have incomes of less than $50,000 a year.
The poll surveyed 1,009 investors between Jan. 11 and 18, with additional interviews of young and new investors.
Most investors, 54 percent, said these are "good times" for investing in stocks, while only 9 percent said this was a bad time to invest.
Nasdaq said investors were only slightly more optimistic on that question now than they were in a June 1988 poll conducted for Nasdaq after the October 1987 stock market crash.
The survey indicated that 54 percent of investors would not make any major changes in their stock holdings in case of a significant stock market decline.
"These people are in for the long haul. They are very much under control," said Peter Hart, president of the research firm conducting the survey. "I don't expect a widescale pullout."
Of those surveyed, 44 percent said they invest in stocks and mutual funds because "over the long run, stocks consistently outperform other investments."
Only 6 percent said they were attracted to stocks because of the recent runup in prices.

The results showed investors banking on their personal investments as the basis for their retirement security, with 41 percent predicting that most of their retirement money will come from savings and investments.

Only 25 percent expect to rely mainly on pensions, while just 4 percent say they will depend mostly on Social Security. Another 24 percent said they will rely equally on all three of those sources during retirement.
"People are intensely aware of the fact that they need to rely on themselves for their financial future," said Alfred Berkeley, Nasdaq president.
So-called Generation Xers, those age 18 to 34, make up about a fifth of all investors.

And despite their lack of faith in Social Security -- just 2 percent of them see it as a primary means of support in old age -- a majority of young investors remained confident that they will be able to retire with financial security.
Indeed, 39 percent of young investors said they see themselves retiring at 55 or younger. Only 26 percent of their "baby boomer" counterparts see themselves retiring so early.
The survey indicated that mutual funds have been a driving force behind the explosive growth in stock ownership among the general public.
Fully 88 percent of investors surveyed said they own shares in one or more mutual funds, up from 60 percent in 1990. Of those who own shares in funds, 69 percent say their holdings exceed $10,000.
